items.why_watch: Max Miller digs into a 4,000-year-old Sumerian clay tablet complaint letter — essentially history's first recorded bad business review — and then actually bakes the cake that era's merchants would have eaten. It's a neat pairing of archaeology and cooking that makes ancient Mesopotamia feel genuinely tangible rather than abstract. If you've ever wondered what a Bronze Age snack tasted like, this is your answer.

Welcome to the History Guy Podcast: Counterfactuals. What is a counterfactual? At it’s most basic, it is a ‘what if’. It’s a way of understanding history as it is by discussing what it could have been.

On today’s episode, we talk about a little remembered campaign by the Alli
items.why_watch: The History Guy turns his attention to the Polar Bear Expedition — the little-known 1918–1919 American military intervention in Arctic Russia that most history classes skip entirely — and uses the counterfactual format to ask what a different outcome might have changed about early Soviet history. At 70 minutes it's a genuine commitment, but the podcast format means it plays well as background listening for anyone curious about forgotten Cold War precursors.

=====

This video explores what attention really is, what role it plays in learning and why people can't multitask - the issue of attention residue.

🕒 OUTLINE:
0:00 - Sneak peek
0:20 - Introduction
0:57
items.why_watch: Harvard neuroscience PhD student Artem Kirsanov explains in under seven minutes why multitasking is neurologically impossible — not just hard, but structurally ruled out by how attention actually works in the brain. He's precise without being jargon-heavy, and the practical implication (that task-switching has a real cognitive cost you're probably underestimating) is the kind of thing that quietly changes how you schedule your day.

items.title: Visiting the Magnificent Shrine of IMAM ALI (AS) | Najaf TRAVEL VLOG | TFT
items.description:
My first day in Najaf, Iraq was an absolute dream! We kicked off the trip by getting lost in the bustling local markets, soaking in the sights, sounds, and vibrant street life of the city. Afterwards, I made my way to the magnificent Shrine of Imam Ali (AS)—an truly breathtaking experience that lived up to all expectations. Above all, the warmth and generosity of the local people made me feel instantly at home. The hospitality here is unmatched!
If you enjoyed this glimpse into Najaf, please giv
items.why_watch: Najaf's Shrine of Imam Ali is one of the most visited pilgrimage sites on earth, yet almost no Western travel content covers it with genuine curiosity and respect — this vlog does both. The creator moves naturally between the chaotic local markets and the shrine's staggering interior, and the interactions with locals give the city a warmth that pure architecture footage never would. It's a useful corrective if your mental image of Iraq is limited to news footage.

global_silver_linings.snippet: A Japanese pharma company has developed a drug that treats the root cause of a leading form of narcolepsy, and is celebrating as it becomes the first of its kind to receive American FDA approval. Narcolepsy type-1 afflicts 120,000 people in the US, and is characterized by sudden bouts of intense daytime drowsiness, disrupted nighttime […] The post US Approves First Drug That Targets Root Cause of Narcolepsy Rather Than its Symptoms appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: For the first time, people living with narcolepsy have a treatment that addresses the actual cause of their condition rather than just masking it — a landmark shift that could transform daily life for hundreds of thousands of people. It's a reminder that medical science, at its best, keeps pushing toward real cures rather than settling for management alone.

global_silver_linings.snippet: It’s a sight that stops Florida boaters and beachgoers in their tracks: a thick green sludge coating the water, smelling of rotten eggs and dead fish. Ashley Smyth, a coastal biogeochemist at the University of Florida, likens the color and consistency to guacamole. “I used to say pea soup, but...
global_silver_linings.reason: Shellfish farming is emerging as a surprisingly elegant, nature-led solution to Florida's toxic algal blooms, with oysters and clams naturally filtering the excess nutrients that fuel the problem. Harnessing what ecosystems already know how to do is exactly the kind of grounded, hopeful thinking our waterways need.
